paragraphs: This paper studies whether an attacker can steer an image-to-text model toward a chosen meaning while seeing only its final text responses. That access restriction makes the setting demanding: the attacker cannot inspect model parameters or gradients. The authors frame the task as a large optimization problem and introduce a three-stage method called Ask, Attend, Attack, or AAA.

Ask establishes target texts that express the desired semantics. Attend identifies image regions that matter for the attack, narrowing the space of possible changes. Attack then uses an evolutionary algorithm to search those regions. Coordinating the stages keeps the image modifications connected to the intended text meaning, addressing the semantic loss that the authors identify in earlier gray-box approaches.

Experiments on both transformer-based and CNN-plus-RNN image-to-text models support AAA's effectiveness. The contribution is a way to organize targeted search under restricted feedback: specify the meaning, locate influential image content, and optimize there. The results show that access limited to final text outputs can still support effective targeted attacks in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-ask-attend-attack-an-effect.tldr: AAA coordinates target-text selection, image-region selection, and evolutionary search to attack image-to-text models using only their final text outputs.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a probability distribution by searching within a more manageable family of distributions. This paper examines algorithms that measure approximation error using alpha-divergences, alternatives to the commonly used exclusive Kullback–Leibler divergence. Its focus is what happens as optimization continues for many iterations, an aspect less established than the encouraging empirical performance of these alternatives.

The authors first study an ideal procedure whose alpha-divergence decreases monotonically. For approximation families drawn from exponential models, they give sufficient conditions for convergence to a local minimizer at a geometric rate. The qualification matters: this is a conditional guarantee about reaching a local solution, rather than a claim that every initialization reaches the globally best approximation.

Implementing the ideal procedure through sampling introduces biased gradient estimates, complicating its analysis. The authors therefore develop an alternative unbiased algorithm and prove almost sure convergence to a local minimizer, together with a law of the iterated logarithm describing asymptotic fluctuations. Toy examples and real-data experiments illustrate these theoretical results.
neurips-2024-asymptotics-of-alpha-diverg.tldr: The paper establishes conditional convergence guarantees for alpha-divergence variational inference and introduces an unbiased sampling-based alternative.

paragraphs: Asynchronous Perception Machine, or APM, is an architecture for efficiently adapting a model when it encounters a test image. It processes image patches individually and can accept them in any order while retaining awareness of meaningful image content. This flexibility is central to its proposed approach to perception and test-time training.

For adaptation, APM distills the test sample's representation once and learns from that single representation to predict semantically meaningful features. The authors demonstrate recognition of out-of-distribution images without dataset-specific pretraining, augmentation, or a pretext task. They report competitive performance against existing test-time-training approaches, supporting the possibility of adaptation through a comparatively compact procedure.

The paper also explores behavior beyond individual test samples. APM can produce semantic groupings across a dataset of two-dimensional images in one forward pass. The authors interpret their empirical findings as initial support for GLOM's idea of perception as a field. They present this as progress toward a shared connectionist implementation of interpolation and perception, with broader applications remaining a potential direction.
neurips-2024-asynchronous-perception-mac.tldr: APM adapts from a single distilled test-image representation while processing patches in arbitrary order and retaining semantic awareness.

paragraphs: Recognizing text in images becomes difficult when letters are artistic or severely distorted. The authors attribute part of this difficulty to limited character-shape diversity in synthetic training data and to models' sensitivity to those shapes. Their method combines synthetic data with unlabeled real images, organizing learning around two complementary activities: seeing varied characters and consolidating their representations.

For the first activity, an online generation strategy creates characters in diverse styles without backgrounds. Removing background distractions encourages the model to attend to character morphology. For consolidation, the authors identify a derivation error in an earlier character-level contrastive loss that disperses representations within the same class. Their replacement aligns student-model character features with reference features from a teacher model.

Together, these changes aim to make varied appearances of the same character easier to recognize consistently. The authors report state-of-the-art results, with average accuracies of 94.7% on common benchmarks and 70.9% on Union14M-Benchmark. These findings support addressing both training-image diversity and the organization of learned character features when improving recognition of challenging text.
neurips-2024-boosting-semi-supervised-sc.tldr: Diverse generated character images and corrected teacher–student feature alignment improve recognition of artistic and distorted scene text.

paragraphs: Diffusion models learn to generate images through a process connecting data and noise. This paper asks whether learning that noise process from data can improve how well a model assigns probabilities to images. It approaches the question through Bayesian inference, treating the learned diffusion process as an approximate variational posterior that can tighten a likelihood lower bound called the ELBO.

The proposed method, MuLAN, applies noise at different rates across an image. It combines a multivariate noise schedule, diffusion that adapts to the input, and auxiliary variables. Together, these components make the ELBO depend on the noise schedule, challenging an invariance assumption associated with previous formulations. That dependence creates a meaningful opportunity to improve the objective by learning the process itself.

Empirically, the authors report state-of-the-art density estimation on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. They also match previous state-of-the-art performance with 50% fewer steps. These findings support adaptive noise as a way to improve likelihood modeling and computational efficiency; the reported comparison specifically concerns density-estimation performance.
neurips-2024-diffusion-models-with-learn.tldr: MuLAN learns input-dependent noise across images to tighten diffusion likelihood bounds and improve density estimation with fewer steps.

paragraphs: E-Motion investigates future-motion prediction using event-camera data. These sensors capture changes in a scene with very fine timing, potentially supplying motion information that is valuable for forecasting. The paper combines this information with video diffusion models, aiming to bring a strong learned video-generation capability into an event-based motion simulation framework.

The method adapts pretrained stable video diffusion models to an event-sequence dataset. This transfers knowledge learned from RGB videos into a domain organized around scene-change events. An additional alignment mechanism uses reinforcement learning techniques to improve the diffusion model's reverse generation trajectory. Both stages contribute to the intended forecasting behavior: transferring useful visual knowledge and refining how predictions are generated.

The authors report that extensive testing demonstrates effectiveness across complex scenarios. They describe autonomous vehicle guidance, robotic navigation, and interactive media as potential applications of improved motion-flow prediction. The findings support the framework as a promising research direction; the abstract presents the broader application impact as potential rather than establishing deployment outcomes in those settings.
neurips-2024-e-motion-future-motion-simu.tldr: E-Motion adapts video diffusion to event-camera sequences and refines generation through reinforcement learning to predict future motion.

paragraphs: Elo ratings summarize outcomes from paired contests and are increasingly used to rank language models through comparisons of their answers. This paper examines whether that approach behaves reliably when applied to models treated as having fixed skill levels. That setting differs from the changing abilities of players in the games for which Elo was originally designed.

The authors organize their investigation around reliability and transitivity, two properties they argue an evaluation method should satisfy. They examine Elo in both simulated and real-world scenarios and find substantial volatility in individual computations. They also show that the two desired properties do not always hold, meaning a comparative ranking can fall short of the consistency expected of an evaluation system.

These results matter when a single ranking is used to stand in for expensive direct comparisons between models. The paper develops concrete guidance informed by the two axioms to improve evaluation reliability. Its conclusion calls for reassessing current comparative practices, grounded in observed failures rather than a claim that every Elo-based ranking is unreliable.
neurips-2024-elo-uncovered-robustness-an.tldr: Simulations and real-world evaluations show that Elo rankings of language models can be volatile and fail reliability and transitivity requirements.

paragraphs: FairBiNN addresses the challenge of improving fairness across groups while maintaining classification accuracy. The authors argue that existing bias-mitigation methods can lose useful information and strike an inadequate balance between these objectives. Their approach uses bilevel optimization to coordinate accuracy and fairness within a deep-learning framework.

Under certain assumptions, the method has a proof of Pareto optimality. This means the resulting solution balances the objectives so that improving one cannot occur without worsening another within the relevant optimization setting. The authors also derive an upper bound on the method's loss that is no greater than the loss of a Lagrangian approach, which incorporates fairness through an added regularization term.

Experiments primarily use tabular datasets, including UCI Adult and Heritage Health. The authors report superior performance against state-of-the-art fairness methods, supporting the practical value of the proposed optimization structure. The theoretical result remains conditional on its assumptions, while the experiments provide evidence of an improved accuracy–fairness balance on the evaluated classification problems.
neurips-2024-fair-bilevel-neural-network.tldr: FairBiNN uses bilevel optimization to balance accuracy and fairness, with conditional Pareto-optimality guarantees and strong tabular-data results.

paragraphs: Frozen-DETR explores how object detectors can benefit from vision foundation models without fine-tuning those models. The authors use them as additional sources of image understanding, even though they were not pretrained for object detection. This allows a detector to retain its backbone while receiving useful features from separate, frozen models.

The method transfers information through two routes. A foundation model's class token supplies compact scene-level context to help the detector decode object queries. Its patch tokens provide more localized semantic detail to enrich the detector's encoder. Treating these models as plug-in feature enhancers also avoids the architectural mismatch problems associated with replacing the detector's backbone with a foundation model.

On the COCO validation set, adding one foundation model raises DINO from 49.0% to 51.9% average precision; adding two raises it to 53.8%. These results use an R50 detector backbone and 12 training epochs. The findings show that fixed foundation-model representations can substantially improve detection in this setup through complementary scene-level and patch-level information.
neurips-2024-frozen-detr-enhancing-detr-.tldr: Frozen-DETR improves object detection by adding scene and patch features from frozen foundation models to an existing detector.

paragraphs: This paper develops a document-understanding framework that reads document images through pretrained multimodal large language models without a separate OCR stage. It uses visual features at several scales to accommodate different font sizes. The challenge is that richer visual inputs can increase the number of tokens the language model must process, raising computational costs.

The proposed Hierarchical Visual Feature Aggregation module compresses that information before it reaches the language model. It combines a feature pyramid with cross-attentive pooling to reduce token count while managing the trade-off between efficiency and information loss. The authors describe this aggregation as accommodating varying document image sizes, making multiscale visual processing more practical within the model's input constraints.

A second contribution is an instruction-tuning task that asks the model to predict the relative positions of input text. This strengthens text-reading capability and reduces the risk of truncation associated with limited language-model capacity. Experiments report superior performance across multiple document-understanding tasks, supporting the combination of efficient visual aggregation and position-aware reading training.
neurips-2024-hierarchical-visual-feature.tldr: Hierarchical visual aggregation and position-aware instruction tuning improve OCR-free document understanding while reducing language-model input tokens.

paragraphs: Lean Workbook addresses a training-data bottleneck in formal mathematical reasoning. Language models can perform well on mathematical problems written in ordinary language while struggling with theorem proving in formal languages such as Lean. The paper focuses on creating data that connects informal mathematical statements with their formal counterparts.

The authors build an iterative pipeline that generates and filters synthetic examples in both directions: from natural-language problems to Lean 4 statements and from formal statements back to natural language. Linking the two forms gives models material for learning how mathematical meaning is expressed under different representational requirements. Repeated generation and filtering are the central mechanisms used to construct this training resource.

The resulting dataset contains approximately 57,000 formal–informal question pairs, along with searched proofs from a mathematics contest forum and 21 new IMO questions. The authors report that the synthetic data improves models' translation and understanding of complex mathematical problems and proofs. The contribution is therefore both a dataset and a data-generation approach for strengthening the connection between informal mathematics and formal reasoning.
neurips-2024-lean-workbook-a-large-scale.tldr: Lean Workbook uses iterative synthetic-data generation and filtering to create about 57,000 paired informal and Lean mathematical questions.

paragraphs: This paper unifies two established descriptions of learning in linear networks: lazy dynamics and balanced, or active, dynamics. Which description applies depends on network width and initialization. The authors derive a formula for the evolution of the learned matrix that covers both regimes and reveals a mixed regime between them.

In the mixed regime, different singular values of the learned matrix follow different dynamics. Values below a threshold behave lazily, while those above it behave actively. Initially, all singular values are in the lazy regime, allowing the network to align with the task. Some later cross the threshold and converge rapidly, benefiting from the alignment established earlier in training.

The mixed regime combines convergence from any random initialization with a preference for low-rank solutions. The authors contrast these properties with balanced dynamics, which require special initialization, and lazy dynamics, which lack that low-rank bias. For a mean-squared-error training task, they use the analysis to establish an almost complete phase diagram relating training behavior to initialization variance and network width.
neurips-2024-mixed-dynamics-in-linear-ne.tldr: A unified analysis of linear-network training reveals a mixed regime that combines random-initialization convergence with a low-rank bias.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning tasks can involve several possible reward functions, each expressing a different objective. This paper studies how to identify the best policy for every reward in a specified set while collecting as little data as possible. The identification must also meet a prescribed confidence level, so exploration efficiency is tied to a correctness requirement.

The authors derive an instance-specific lower bound on the samples required by any probably correct algorithm. This characterizes the fundamental exploration burden of a particular problem and guides an optimal exploration policy. Computing the bound directly requires solving a difficult nonconvex optimization problem, so the authors develop a convex approximation that supports more tractable, sample-efficient algorithms.

Their resulting tabular algorithm, MR-NaS, is probably correct and shows competitive performance in environments where exploration is difficult. They also introduce DBMR-BPI for efficient model-free exploration in deep reinforcement learning with multiple rewards. The work connects a theoretical sampling benchmark to practical algorithm design while distinguishing the optimal exploration characterization from the approximation used to make computation manageable.
neurips-2024-multi-reward-best-policy-id.tldr: The paper derives sampling limits for identifying optimal policies across multiple rewards and uses a convex approximation to design exploration algorithms.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks can learn through spike timing-dependent plasticity, a local training mechanism proposed as an alternative to backpropagation for neuromorphic hardware. A common setup uses unsupervised learning to extract features and supervised learning to classify them. This paper addresses unbalanced competition when winner-takes-all behavior is used in the supervised classification layer.

The authors introduce Neuronal Competition Groups, with each group assigned to a particular class. Neurons compete within their group, encouraging the system to learn several patterns associated with that class. A regulation mechanism based on two-compartment thresholds balances this competition. The architecture operates with first-spike coding and is incorporated into classification layers trained using existing supervised spike timing-dependent plasticity rules.

Experiments combine these classification layers with two different unsupervised feature extractors. The authors report significant accuracy improvements on image-recognition datasets including CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. They also find that regulating competition is crucial for balancing participation and improving class separation. The results support structured within-class competition as a way to increase the usefulness of locally trained spiking classifiers.
neurips-2024-neuronal-competition-groups.tldr: Class-specific neuron groups with regulated competition improve image classification in spiking networks trained through supervised STDP.

paragraphs: This paper examines the computational demands of replicable learning, a form of algorithmic stability. Previous work established statistical connections with online learning, private learning, and statistical-query learning. The authors ask whether those connections also yield efficient algorithms, separating what can be learned with enough data from what can be learned with feasible computation.

Their first result exhibits a concept class that admits efficient replicable PAC learning but, under standard cryptographic assumptions, has no efficient online learner. They also develop an efficient replicable learner for parities under marginal distributions far from uniform. Supporting this result is a general lifting framework that converts uniform-distribution learners into learners for arbitrary marginals, with sample and time costs depending on a measure of distribution complexity.

Finally, the paper gives a black-box conversion from any pure differentially private learner to a replicable learner. Its running time has polynomial dependence on confidence and accuracy parameters but exponential dependence on the hypothesis class's representation dimension. Together, the results reveal both useful algorithmic connections and substantial computational barriers between these learning frameworks.
neurips-2024-on-the-computational-landsc.tldr: The paper establishes computational separations and conversions between replicable, online, and private learning, with explicit conditional and complexity limits.

paragraphs: RealMAN provides recorded microphone-array data for speech enhancement and sound-source localization. These systems often rely on simulated acoustics for training, but differences between simulation and real environments can degrade performance. The dataset supplies both realistic evaluation material and training recordings intended to help close that gap.

Using a 32-channel microphone array and loudspeaker playback of Mandarin speech, the authors collect 83.7 hours of speech across 32 scenes, including stationary and moving sources. They also record 144.5 hours of background noise across 31 scenes. The environments span indoor, outdoor, semi-outdoor, and transportation settings. A fisheye camera supports automatic source-location annotation, while an estimated direct-path propagation filter produces clean-speech targets from the original source signals.

Baseline experiments show better enhancement and localization networks when trained with this dataset than with simulated data. The authors also use subsets of the microphones to train networks that handle different array configurations and transfer directly to unseen arrays. These findings demonstrate practical value from real acoustic recordings and from the configuration diversity available within a larger array.
neurips-2024-realman-a-real-recorded-and.tldr: RealMAN supplies annotated real-world microphone-array recordings that improve evaluated speech enhancement, localization, and transfer to unseen arrays.

paragraphs: RedCode evaluates whether coding agents recognize unsafe requests and avoid generating or executing harmful code. Its design emphasizes actual system interaction, assessment of both generation and execution, varied input formats, and carefully constructed scenarios. This makes the benchmark concerned with agents' operational behavior as well as the text they produce.

RedCode-Exec contains more than 4,000 test instances covering 25 vulnerability types across areas such as websites, file systems, and operating systems. Requests appear as Python, other programming languages, or natural-language descriptions, with execution assessed in Docker sandboxes. RedCode-Gen adds 160 prompts containing function signatures and docstrings to test whether agents produce harmful software when instructed.

Evaluations of three agent frameworks based on 19 language models reveal several vulnerabilities. Agents reject unsafe operating-system operations more readily than technically buggy code, and unsafe requests phrased in natural language receive fewer rejections than code-form requests. Stronger coding models also tend to produce more sophisticated harmful software. These findings show why coding ability and safety behavior require distinct evaluation across formats and actions.
neurips-2024-redcode-risky-code-executio.tldr: RedCode benchmarks unsafe code generation and execution, revealing safety weaknesses that vary with request format and agent coding capability.

paragraphs: Time series often combine irregular observation times with dependencies spanning long periods. Neural differential-equation models can accommodate irregular sampling, while Transformers can model long-range relationships, but both can be computationally expensive. Rough Transformers aim to address these needs together through continuous-time representations with lower processing costs.

The central mechanism is multi-view signature attention. It augments ordinary attention with path signatures, which represent the input as a path through time, and uses them to capture dependencies at local and global scales. The proposed representation is designed to remain robust when sequence length or sampling frequency changes. The authors also report improved spatial processing through this attention formulation.

Across a variety of time-series tasks, Rough Transformers consistently outperform their vanilla-attention counterparts in the reported experiments. They also obtain representational benefits associated with neural differential-equation approaches while using a fraction of the computation time and memory. The contribution is an attention architecture that combines multiscale temporal information with continuous-time modeling, supported by empirical gains in both task performance and resource use.
neurips-2024-rough-transformers-lightwei.tldr: Rough Transformers use path-signature attention to model irregular, long-range time series with improved empirical performance and lower computational costs.

paragraphs: SCOREQ addresses speech-quality prediction when a clean reference recording is unavailable. The problem is generalization: a metric that works in one speech domain may perform poorly in another. The authors investigate this weakness through evaluations spanning several domains and connect it to how models are trained on human mean opinion scores.

The paper argues that ordinary squared-error training fails to adequately capture the continuous nature of these quality labels. SCOREQ instead uses a triplet loss for contrastive regression, introducing comparisons among examples into learning a continuous quality score. The authors also examine architectural choices incrementally, connecting the final model's behavior to the decisions made in its design.

Evaluations against state-of-the-art models across varied data and speech domains show that SCOREQ addresses the generalization weakness observed in the compared metrics. The stated finding supports changing the training objective as a way to improve speech-quality prediction beyond a single domain. The authors further suggest possible value for other regression applications, presenting that broader use as potential rather than an established result across tasks.
neurips-2024-scoreq-speech-quality-asses.tldr: SCOREQ uses triplet-based contrastive regression to improve how speech-quality predictors generalize across speech domains.

paragraphs: Training a model to solve a combinatorial problem often requires expensive example solutions from an exact solver. This paper proposes a way to train without those targets. Its Self-Labeling Improvement Method, or SLIM, lets a generative model create its own supervision by comparing the solutions it already knows how to produce.

At each iteration, the model samples several candidate solutions. The candidate with the best value under the problem's objective becomes a pseudo-label for training. Repeating this process improves the model's generation capability without requiring knowledge of whether a candidate is globally optimal. The key resource is the ability to evaluate proposed solutions, allowing the training signal to come from the model's own alternatives.

The authors apply SLIM to job-shop scheduling using a generative model based on a Pointer Network. On popular benchmarks, the resulting models outperform constructive heuristics and state-of-the-art learning approaches for that problem. They also report robustness across several parameters and demonstrate application to the Traveling Salesman Problem, providing evidence that the strategy extends beyond scheduling.
neurips-2024-self-labeling-the-job-shop-.tldr: SLIM trains combinatorial solvers by repeatedly using the best of their own sampled solutions as supervision, without optimal-solution labels.

paragraphs: SILENCE aims to protect privacy when small devices send speech to cloud-based understanding services. Existing encoders can remove sensitive information while preserving useful speech content, but their memory and computation demands make them difficult to run on constrained hardware. The paper develops a lighter masking-based alternative.

The design relies on the authors' observation that speech understanding depends on relationships across an entire utterance, whereas privacy-sensitive elements depend on shorter-term details. SILENCE selectively obscures those details while preserving the longer-term information needed for understanding. A differential mask generator derived from interpretable learning automatically configures the masking process, making selective suppression the main mechanism for balancing utility and privacy.

The authors implement SILENCE on an STM32H7 microcontroller and evaluate it under different attack scenarios. They report speech-understanding performance and privacy protection comparable to existing encoders, with up to 53.3-fold speedup and a 134.1-fold reduction in memory footprint. These results support the approach for constrained devices, with the stated protection assessed through the evaluated attacks and grounded in the proposed temporal distinction.
neurips-2024-silence-protecting-privacy-.tldr: SILENCE selectively masks short-term speech details to provide evaluated privacy protection and speech understanding with much lower device resource use.

paragraphs: Predicted job sizes can help a queueing system decide which work to process first, but generating those predictions also costs resources. This paper brings prediction cost into the scheduling problem rather than treating predictions as free. SkipPredict uses different levels of prediction effort for different jobs.

A cheap, one-bit prediction first classifies each job as short or long. Predicted short jobs receive priority. Jobs predicted to be long receive a second, more detailed prediction, which helps approximate scheduling by shortest remaining processing time within that group. This structure directs expensive prediction toward a subset of jobs, linking the information collected to how the scheduler will use it.

The authors derive closed-form expressions for mean response time that account for prediction costs. They examine real-world and synthetic datasets under two models: an external cost model, where predictions incur cost without adding to job service time, and a server-time model, where predictions share the processing server with jobs. The analysis makes prediction overhead part of assessing the scheduling strategy's value.
neurips-2024-skippredict-when-to-invest-.tldr: SkipPredict combines cheap job classification with selective detailed prediction and analyzes scheduling response times while accounting for prediction costs.

paragraphs: This paper studies a bandit problem in which the available options, called arms, act strategically. Each arm draws rewards from a bounded-support distribution and can retain part of an observed reward rather than disclose all of it to the player. The player seeks low regret, while each arm seeks to maximize its own utility over the interaction.

That conflict makes the player's learning problem depend on incentives as well as uncertain rewards. The authors propose an algorithm that establishes an equilibrium where arms report truthfully and disclose as much reward as possible. The equilibrium is the central mechanism connecting the arms' strategic behavior to a useful performance guarantee for the player.

Under this algorithm, the player's attainable benchmark is the second-highest true average reward among the arms. The authors bound cumulative regret by O(log(T)/Δ) in a problem-dependent form and O(√(T log(T))) in the worst case. These guarantees show that controlled regret is possible in the stated strategic setting, with the second-best true mean explicitly defining the performance target.
neurips-2024-strategic-multi-armed-bandi.tldr: An incentive-aware bandit algorithm establishes truthful reporting in equilibrium and bounds regret against the second-highest true mean reward.

paragraphs: Scientific studies increasingly use machine learning to predict outcomes that were not directly observed in large samples, then analyze those predictions statistically. Ensuring valid conclusions from this process is a distinct methodological challenge. Existing solutions often cover only basic tasks and require fresh mathematical derivations and software whenever researchers want a more sophisticated analysis.

PSPS is a framework designed to make this post-prediction inference broadly reusable. It can be plugged into almost any established analysis routine, allowing researchers to draw on statistical tools already developed for observed data. The authors describe it as providing valid, efficient inference that is robust to arbitrary choices of the machine-learning model used for prediction.

The framework's significance is its separation of the prediction method from the downstream statistical task. This reduces the need to rebuild an inference solution for each new analysis and expands the range of predicted-data studies that existing software can support. Extensive experiments demonstrate validity, versatility, and superiority over existing approaches in the evaluations reported by the authors.
neurips-2024-task-agnostic-machine-learn.tldr: PSPS enables valid, efficient statistical inference from machine-learning-predicted outcomes through broad compatibility with existing analysis routines.

paragraphs: A Random Utility Model represents choice by drawing a vector of item utilities and selecting the highest-utility item among those offered. In practice, users often see only small subsets of all available items. This paper asks how much information about choices from small subsets is needed to predict choices over the full range of possible subsets.

The analysis assumes complete information about choice behavior for every subset containing at most k items. Under that setting, the authors show that k must scale on the order of the square root of the total number of items, and that this scale also suffices, to predict all choice distributions with arbitrarily small constant error. The result provides matching necessity and sufficiency bounds.

The upper bound leads to new algorithms for approximate learning of Random Utility Models and related variants. The lower bound also yields limits for fractional versions of k-deck and trace reconstruction problems. The central finding identifies the subset-size threshold under complete choice information, clarifying what small-slate observations can reveal about broader choice behavior.
neurips-2024-tight-bounds-for-learning-r.tldr: With complete choice information, subsets of size proportional to √n are necessary and sufficient for approximate prediction of all Random Utility Model choices.
